clinicalPearls: A recognised progression of polycythaemia vera to a myelofibrotic phase with marrow fibrosis
It is marked by a falling need for venesection, anaemia, progressive splenomegaly and constitutional symptoms
The blood film shows a leucoerythroblastic picture with teardrop cells
Diagnostic criteria require established polycythaemia vera plus marrow fibrosis and additional features such as anaemia and splenomegaly
It resembles primary myelofibrosis clinically and shares the risk of leukaemic transformation
Management mirrors that of myelofibrosis, including JAK inhibition for symptoms and splenomegaly and transplantation in selected patients
reference.pathophysiology: Post-polycythaemia vera myelofibrosis represents clonal evolution of the underlying JAK2-driven myeloproliferative neoplasm. Chronic cytokine release and megakaryocyte proliferation stimulate reactive deposition of reticulin and collagen fibrosis in the marrow, progressively impairing haematopoiesis. As the marrow fails, red cell production falls (so venesection is no longer needed and anaemia develops) and haematopoiesis shifts to the spleen and liver (extramedullary haematopoiesis), causing organomegaly and the leucoerythroblastic blood picture. The disease carries an increased risk of transformation to acute leukaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Reactive marrow fibrosis (for example infection, malignancy)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and film for leucoerythroblastic changes and teardrop cells
JAK2 and driver-mutation status (usually known from prior PV)
Assessment of spleen size and constitutional symptoms
redFlags: Rising blasts indicating transformation to acute leukaemia
Profound constitutional symptoms and weight loss
reference.prognosis: Transformation to a fibrotic phase generally worsens prognosis compared with polycythaemia vera, with outcomes similar to primary myelofibrosis and a risk of leukaemic transformation; allogeneic transplantation is the only cure.
pitfalls: Attributing the falling haematocrit and anaemia to over-venesection rather than fibrotic transformation
Confusing it with primary myelofibrosis without the prior PV history
Overlooking the need to reassess prognosis and management
management: Management mirrors primary myelofibrosis and is risk-stratified with a prognostic score to guide intensity
JAK inhibition with ruxolitinib to reduce symptomatic splenomegaly and constitutional symptoms
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, the only curative option, for eligible higher-risk patients
Manage anaemia with transfusion support and agents such as erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, danazol or immunomodulators, as venesection is no longer required
Symptom-directed care for splenomegaly, with splenectomy or splenic irradiation in selected refractory cases
Monitor blood counts and spleen size and surveil for leukaemic transformation
Supportive care including infection prevention and management of transfusion-related iron overload, within haematology-led multidisciplinary care with transplant assessment
